newsitem.title: INDIA: India banks' bad debts seen reduced in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: India banks' bad debts seen reduced in 1996/97.

text.p: India's state-owned banks are expected to have reduced their non-performing assets (NPAs) as a proportion of total advances to 13.6 percent at the end of 1996/97 (April-March), a parliamentary panel said on Tuesday.
The ratio of NPAs to total advances of the banks stood at 17.12 percent at the end of 1995/96.

"These NPAs as at the end of March, 1997 are expected to decline to 13.6 percent of the total advances," the standing committee of deputies on the Finance Ministry said in a report presented to parliament.
The NPAs mainly represent bad debts or unproductive loans.
The panel expressed concern at the huge amount of NPAs of state-owned banks estimated at 400 billion rupees ($11.2 billion) at the end of 1996/97.
"These figures are much more higher if interest accumulated on NPAs is taken into account," the report said.
Funds blocked in bad debts, if recovered, can be used for development of economy, it said.
The panel urged the government to set up a committee, consisting of the governor of the central bank and bankers, to suggest ways to improve the recovery of loans not repaid.

The panel said the reduction in NPAs in 1996/97 was likely as banks were increasingly deploying their funds in zero-risk government securities instead of lending them to the corporate sector, where the risk is higher.
This was one of the factors contributing to an industrial slowdown, the panel said.
India's industry grew 8.3 percent in the nine months to December in 1996/97 compared with 11.4 percent in the corresponding period in the previous year.
"The committee also desire that the government should examine the need for setting up of more debt recovery tribunals to expedite recovery of bank's dues," the report said.

The state-owned banks should shrug off their inertia and start lending in a big way to accelerate economic growth, the report said, apparently referring to a slowdown in corporate lending by cautious banks.
"The committee doubts whether any of the public sector banks extend loans to even the best rated corporates at their prime lending rates," it said.

India has begun to encourage the setting up of private sector banks under an economic reform programme launched in 1991, but the bulk of the banking system is still under the influence of banks nationalised under socialist policies between 1969 and 1978.
